qt: to the Commission Ilaria Salis (The Left), Mimmo Lucano (The Left), Cristina Guarda (Verts/ALE), Ignazio Roberto Marino (Verts/ALE), Leoluca Orlando (Verts/ALE), Benedetta Scuderi (Verts/ALE), Danilo Della Valle (The Left), Mario Furore (The Left), Carolina Morace (The Left), Valentina Palmisano (The Left), Gaetano Pedulla' (The Left), Dario Tamburrano (The Left), Pasquale Tridico (The Left), Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D), Marco Tarquinio (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Annalisa Corrado (S&D), Giuseppe Lupo (S&D), Cecilia Strada (S&D), Camilla Laureti (S&D), Damien Carême (The Left), Per Clausen (The Left), Estrella Galán (The Left), Leila Chaibi (The Left), Catarina Martins (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left), Anthony Smith (The Left), Manon Aubry (The Left), Pernando Barrena Arza (The Left), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Isabel Serra Sánchez (The Left), Rima Hassan (The Left), Majdouline Sbai (Verts/ALE), Mounir Satouri (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Lena Schilling (Verts/ALE) Subject:

The Italy-Libya Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), signed in 2017 and set to renew automatically on 2 November 2025, has enabled systematic pushbacks, arbitrary detention, torture, sexual violence, forced labour and other severe abuses against migrants and refugees in Libya. Despite extensive evidence from the UN and numerous NGOs, including Refugees in Libya, showing that the EU- and Italy-trained Libyan Coast Guard have committed serious human rights violations, the Commission continues to justify this cooperation as a means of engagement to improve the situation1. Recent incidents deepen concerns: on 12 October 2025, 140 people disembarked in Pozzallo, Italy after being attacked by Libyan militiamen using Italian-supplied vessels; one person was critically injured, and two others were seriously wounded2. 1.

What is the position of the Commission concerning the continued EU support for Libyan authorities with obligations under international and Eu law, including Articles 18 and 19 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the principle of non-refoulement?
What measures will it take to ensure that EU or Member State funds do not contribute to such violations?
How does the Commission assess the continued implementation of the MoU considering its obligations under EU and international law, and does it consider that any violations have occurred?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.3.2026) Respect for international and human-rights law, including the principle of non-refoulement and the protection of migrants, refugees and asylum-seekers, is at the centre of the EU’s engagement with Libya. EU support to Libyan authorities is intended to improve the protection of migrants and refugees, strengthen rights-based migration management and prevent loss of life at sea and in the desert. Whenever concerns or incidents are reported, the Commission raises them with the Libyan authorities and urges full compliance with national and international obligations. EU support is subject to continuous monitoring through regular reporting by implementing partners, monitoring visits by Commission staff, independent evaluations and, since 2019, a Third-Party Monitoring Framework. In parallel, the Commission maintains a regular technical dialogue with the Libyan authorities, in which compliance with international law and humanrights standards is consistently raised and specific incidents can be discussed. As regards the Italy–Libya Memorandum of Understanding, the Commission recalls, and consistently communicates to Member States, that EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights, needs to be respected in the initiatives they undertake in the field of migration.
